title: Singing the AI Blues: Where Have All the Willie's Gone?
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Terry Underwood uses the blues, with Robert Johnson kneeling at the crossroads as his central image, to describe how many teachers feel as AI models roll through education. He argues that teaching is uncertain, interpretive and emotional, so it cannot be absorbed by bots the way law or medicine can. The busy world around the teacher is not cruel, only hurried, which leaves teachers isolated while administrators and receptionists alike hand communication to bots. Underwood describes a loss of innocence among teachers who were once excited about what AI could do for learning, and a demoralising sense of working without a map or colleagues to adapt with. Even the blue-book exam, he suggests, becomes a lonely act when students do not know why it is required. The piece is a short lament rather than a policy argument, and it closes by recommending the old victrola.
points: The author casts the teacher's position as a lonely crossroads: the world is not hostile to teachers, only too busy and fast-moving to stop.
Teaching is uncertain, interpretive and emotional, which sets it apart from fields like law and medicine where bots can be trained on libraries and records.
Dehumanization, as bot messages replace human exchanges between administrators and teachers, is named as the failure loop of the AI moment.
Teachers who began enthusiastic about AI have lost their innocence, and working without a shared map or collaborators is demoralising.
Practices such as requiring blue-book writing leave some students puzzled, so teachers feel isolated even in the rituals they trust.
quotes: Bob is on his knees in plain sight. Nobody stops. Those drivers aren’t cruel and inhuman. They’re just busy. That’s what 2026 feels like for teachers at all levels.

Teaching isn’t like the law; bots can be trained on law libraries. Teaching isn’t like medicine; bots can surveil patient-doctor interactions and then answer questions the patient has. Teaching is uncertain, interpretive, emotional.
An intergalactic force of bots carry their own sundown sermon: Get on board or get out of the way.
Administrators send out bot messages; return emails are filtered through bot receptionists.
He can no longer do what he knows to do well; he can no longer participate as an innocent in classroom activities. He makes his students write in blue books, and some know why and others don’t.

Teachers who got excited about the opportunities AI affords in learning have lost their innocence. Existing in this newly dark space without lights and a map, without others collaborating to adapt, is demoralizing and makes one blue.
